item.text: {"case_id":"SPR00040","decision":"candidate","candidate_ranking":["C23","C01","C16"],"selected_candidate_label":"C23","confidence":0.98,"relationship_type":"both","rationale":"C23 plausibly supplied a concrete and material template. Both directives reject private bills seeking National Service Life Insurance proceeds for designated beneficiaries outside the pre-August 1, 1946 permitted classes; both discuss an alleged in loco parentis relationship, emphasize that the later statutory change was not retroactive, cite thousands of similarly denied claims, and conclude with nearly identical language about preserving uniformity and equality in veterans' programs. C01 and C16 share the broader veterans-benefits machinery and unusually close uniformity language, but C23 matches the child's specific insurance problem and argumentative sequence much more closely.","shared_material":[{"child_excerpt":"he did not stand in loco parentis to the insured and was therefore not within the permitted classes of beneficiaries, a statutory requirement applicable to National Service life insurance maturing prior to August 1, 1946","parent_excerpt":"Prior to August 1, 1946, the law governing National Service Life Insurance policies did not permit either an aunt or a cousin to be named as a beneficiary. The law did recognize, as proper beneficiaries persons who, under certain circumstances, stood in loco parentis to the insured.","explanation":"The same specialized eligibility rule, cutoff date, insurance program, and in-loco-parentis mechanism form the core legal issue."},{"child_excerpt":"approximately 3,600 claims for the proceeds of National Service life insurance denied by the Veterans' Administration because the claimants were not within the classes of beneficiaries permitted by law","parent_excerpt":"More than 3,200 claims of designated beneficiaries for the proceeds of National Service Life Insurance have been denied because they were not within the permitted classes of beneficiaries.","explanation":"Both use closely parallel administrative statistics to show that individualized relief would discriminate against a large class of similarly situated claimants."},{"child_excerpt":"I am opposed to setting aside the principles and rules of administration prescribed in the general law relating to veterans' benefit programs. Uniformity and equality of treatment to all who are similarly situated must be the steadfast rule if the Federal programs for veterans and their beneficiaries are to be operated successfully.","parent_excerpt":"Far more fundamental is the objection I have heretofore expressed to setting aside the principles and rules of administration prescribed in the general laws governing veterans' benefit programs. Uniformity and equality of treatment to all who are similarly situated must be the rule if the Federal programs for veterans and their beneficiaries are to be operated successfully.","explanation":"This is near-verbatim distinctive language expressing the same governing objection and strongly indicates reuse."}]}
